cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Acknowledge Our History
cards.instruction: Make someone recognize that the relationship, memory, or sacrifice mattered and cannot be treated as incidental.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I haven't approved boxing our allotment photo. That summer deserves more than the back of a cupboard.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: We grew three carrots. I need the shelf.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I approve freeing the shelf, not calling it wasted. You got out of bed every morning to water those carrots with me.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I could put the photo on my desk at work.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: That move is approved. When someone laughs at the harvest, tell them about those mornings. I'm not authorizing a caption that makes it just three carrots.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 denies storage approval, A3 permits shelf clearing but not dismissal and A5 authorizes desk display with a required account of shared mornings, controlling preservation to obtain acknowledgment.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 small harvest/shelf need causes A3 practical permission plus deeper memory; B4 desk solution causes A5 request to tell that meaning there.

relationship.evidence: B2 needs space and B4 offers visible preservation, a helpful solution that A uses rather than blocks.

heightening.evidence: B4 public desk display causes A5 to require a story beyond carrot count for future viewers.

specificity.evidence: A1 allotment photo and B2 harvest make the object clear; A3 daily watering states significance without invented diagnosis.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 authorization of a caption makes memory protection sound like approval authority, but the final wording is somewhat formal.
